concepts.def: Closed system circulating water between atmosphere, land and oceans.
Area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, an open subsystem of the hydrological cycle.
Boundary separating one drainage basin from another.
Combined loss of water from soil (evaporation) and vegetation (transpiration).

walkthroughs.body_html: The global hydrological cycle is a closed system, exchanging no matter with space. About 97% of water is saline; only ~2.5% is fresh, much of it locked in ice and groundwater. Inputs to a drainage basin include precipitation; outputs include channel discharge, evapotranspiration and deep groundwater loss.

Precipitation may intercept vegetation, run overland (especially on saturated or impermeable surfaces), infiltrate into soil, percolate into rock or reach channels through throughflow and groundwater flow. Lag time between rainfall peak and discharge peak depends on basin shape, soils and land use.

Storage includes ice and snow, groundwater, lakes and rivers, soil moisture, and atmospheric water vapour. Residence times vary from days (atmosphere) to thousands of years (deep groundwater). Human activity — dams, irrigation, urbanisation — alters both stores and flows.
